props.title: The Palm Beach Story

sections.content: Preston Sturges crafted the ultimate screwball romance with The Palm Beach Story, a masterpiece of rapid-fire dialogue and absurdist plot twists. Claudette Colbert and Joel McCrea deliver perfect comic timing as Gerry and Tom Jeffers, a married couple whose financial troubles spark an outrageous series of events. The film sits alongside other essential screwball classics like Bringing Up Baby (1938) and The Lady Eve (1941), but Sturges pushes the genre's conventions even further with his signature blend of sophisticated wit and slapstick chaos. The opening sequence alone, with its parallel wedding scenes and unexplained twin subplot, announces this isn't your typical romantic comedy.

sections.content: What sets The Palm Beach Story apart is how it skewers American attitudes about wealth, marriage and class while maintaining genuine affection for its characters. The Wienie King, a hard-of-hearing millionaire who gives Gerry money "because he's rich," exemplifies Sturges' absurdist take on American capitalism. The Ale and Quail Club sequence on the train pushes screwball mayhem to new heights, while anticipating the darker comedy of films like Some Like It Hot (1959). Sturges' trademark ensemble of character actors, including William Demarest and Sig Arno, adds layers of comic genius to every scene.

The film's influence echoes through later romantic comedies like The Seven Year Itch (1955) and Some Like It Hot (1959), which similarly use travel and disguise to explore marriage and identity. Modern films like The Proposal (2009) still draw from its playbook of using wealth disparities and fake relationships as romantic comedy fuel. But few match Sturges' ability to balance sophisticated dialogue with physical comedy while maintaining a sharp satirical edge. SUBHEAD: Screwball Innovation and Social Commentary

sections.content: While most screwball comedies of the era focused on class differences, The Palm Beach Story uniquely examines marriage itself as an economic arrangement. The character of Princess Centimillia (Mary Astor) represents old-world aristocracy colliding with American new money, creating a commentary on marriage as transaction that feels surprisingly modern. This theme would later be explored in films like How to Marry a Millionaire (1953) and Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), though rarely with Sturges' combination of cynicism and warmth.
